subsection: 1. Case study of a developed economy: Ireland

notes.b: Economic activities (the ways people earn a living) are grouped into three sectors by what they do with raw materials or with people's needs. Knowing which sector a job belongs to is the first step in describing any economy.
points: Primary activity is extracting raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry, mining, quarrying and energy extraction. Nothing is made yet, so the resource is simply taken from the land or sea.
Secondary activity is processing raw materials or assembling components (parts) into goods, such as manufacturing, food processing and construction.
Tertiary activity is services, which provide help or access rather than goods, such as retail, banking, tourism, teaching, health, transport and IT (information technology).
Classifying jobs: a miner or forester is primary; a builder is secondary, because construction is secondary; a teacher, banker or tour guide is tertiary.
Some writers add a quaternary sector for research and information, but the three-sector model is used here.
notes.tip: When you classify jobs, remember that construction is secondary, not tertiary, and that forestry and mining are primary. Tourism, banking, teaching and transport are all tertiary.

notes.h: Sectoral change as an economy develops
notes.b: The share of workers in each sector changes as a country becomes richer. Ireland shows the end result of that shift.
points: As an economy develops, employment moves from primary to secondary and then to tertiary activity. This is why primary employment falls as countries develop.
Services employ about three-quarters of Irish workers (2020s), which means Ireland is a tertiary economy; agriculture, forestry and fishing employ about 4–5%.
Census 2022 counted a State population of about 5.1 million; the CSO (Central Statistics Office) Labour Force Survey (2024) recorded over 2.7 million people in employment.
In a developing economy, by contrast, primary employment is high. There is more on this in the Economic Development notes.
notes.tip: If you are asked which country is most developed from employment figures, it is the one with the highest tertiary share. Explain why primary employment falls as countries develop.

notes.b: For its first decades as an independent State, Ireland tried to shelter its own firms from foreign competition. This is the starting point of the timeline of how Ireland became a developed economy.
points: The Control of Manufactures Acts, 1932 and 1934, restricted foreign ownership of Irish firms, so industry stayed in Irish hands.
High tariffs (taxes on imported goods) protected small Irish firms serving the home market, so they had little pressure to become efficient or to export.
The 1950s brought high unemployment and heavy emigration (people leaving the country to live abroad), which showed that protection had not created enough jobs.

notes.h: Free trade and foreign investment, 1949 to 1973
notes.b: From the late 1950s Ireland reversed its policy and opened up to trade and foreign companies. Each step below was meant to bring in jobs and exports.
points: The Industrial Development Authority (IDA) was set up in 1949 to attract industry, so Ireland had an agency for winning new firms.
Export Profits Tax Relief, 1956, removed tax on profits from exports, so firms had a reason to sell abroad.

T.K. Whitaker's Economic Development and the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958) set the policy of free trade, foreign investment and export-led growth (growth driven by selling abroad), carried out under Seán Lemass as Taoiseach from 1959.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) reduced trade barriers with Britain, Ireland's nearest and biggest market.
Ireland joined the EEC (European Economic Community, the forerunner of the EU) on 1 January 1973, together with the UK and Denmark.

notes.h: Education and a growing skilled workforce
notes.b: Attracting foreign firms also needed people with the right skills. Free schooling was the policy that built them.
points: Free second-level education was announced in 1966 by Donogh O'Malley and introduced in 1967.
A better-educated workforce made Ireland attractive to firms that needed skilled labour in the decades that followed.
The IDA became an independent agency under the Industrial Development Act 1969, so it could pursue foreign investment in its own right.

notes.h: Single Market, euro and corporation tax
notes.b: Later steps tied Ireland more closely to Europe and set the tax rates that attract multinational companies. Corporation tax is the tax a company pays on its profits.
points: The EU Single Market began in 1993, giving Irish firms and foreign investors access to the wider EU market without trade barriers.
The euro was adopted in 1999, with notes and coins introduced in 2002, which means Irish firms trade with the eurozone (the countries using the euro) without exchange-rate costs.
Corporation tax on trading profits was 12.5% from 2003. This low rate is a main reason multinationals locate in Ireland.
From 2024 very large multinational groups (global turnover over €750 million) pay a 15% minimum rate under the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) agreement.
notes.tip: The general corporation tax rate is 12.5% from 2003. The 10% rate belongs only to the IFSC in 1987, so never say Ireland's tax is 10% today.

notes.b: The Celtic Tiger is the name for Ireland's period of very rapid growth. It followed from the earlier policies of free trade, investment and education.
points: Rapid growth from the mid-1990s to 2007 was driven first by exports and foreign direct investment (FDI, money invested by foreign firms in Irish plants), especially from US technology and pharmaceutical firms.
A property and construction boom added to growth later in the period, because rising prices encouraged more building.
Unemployment fell to about 4–5% by the mid-2000s, because so many new jobs were created.
Net immigration (more people arriving than leaving) replaced emigration, with large inflows from the new EU states after the 2004 enlargement.

notes.b: The property boom ended in a crash that put Irish banks in danger. The State stepped in to protect them.
points: The property bubble (a rise in prices that could not last) burst in 2007–2008, leaving banks with large bad loans (loans unlikely to be repaid) secured on property that had lost value.
On 30 September 2008 the government guaranteed Irish bank liabilities, promising that the banks' debts would be covered.
Anglo Irish Bank was nationalised (taken into State ownership) in January 2009.
The National Asset Management Agency (NAMA), set up in 2009, took over property loans from the banks.

notes.h: EU–IMF programme and public debt, 2010 to 2013
notes.b: The cost of rescuing the banks left the State unable to borrow normally, so it needed outside help. The crash also hit jobs and population.
points: An EU–IMF (International Monetary Fund) programme was agreed in November 2010, providing €67.5 billion in external loans.
Ireland left the programme in December 2013, which means the State could borrow on normal markets again.
Unemployment peaked at about 16% in early 2012, so net emigration resumed from 2009 to 2014.

Government debt peaked at about 120% of GDP (the value of everything produced in the country in a year) in 2012: the state borrowed to rescue the banks while its tax base (the income and spending that can be taxed) collapsed with the economy.
notes.tip: If asked why the Irish government has a large debt, give both causes: borrowing to rescue the banks, and a collapsed tax base.

notes.b: After 2013 the economy recovered strongly. Jobs returned and public finances improved.
points: Unemployment was about 4–5% in 2023–2024, near full employment (almost everyone who wants work has it).
Budget surpluses (tax income greater than spending) in the 2020s came largely from corporation tax paid by a small number of large multinationals, so public finances depend on them.
COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020–2021 hit tourism, hospitality and retail hardest.

notes.b: When most people who want work have it, the whole economy gains, not only the workers. Each benefit below follows from people earning and spending.
points: Employed people pay income tax, and their spending pays VAT (value-added tax, a tax on goods and services), so tax revenue rises.
Welfare spending falls because fewer people need unemployment payments, so the State has more to spend elsewhere.
Consumer spending by employed people supports jobs in other sectors, such as shops and cafes.
Less emigration keeps skilled people in the economy, so firms can find the workers they need.
Government revenue can pay for investment in infrastructure (roads, rail, utilities) and services.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one benefit of high employment. Pair each benefit with its reason, such as tax revenue rising because workers pay income tax and VAT.

notes.b: Because so many multinationals are based in Ireland, their profits can distort the national figures. This makes GDP a poor guide to how well Irish people are doing.
points: In 2015 Irish GDP grew by about 26% after multinationals moved intellectual property assets (such as patents and software rights) to Ireland; the effect was nicknamed 'leprechaun economics'.
Because GDP is inflated by these profits, the CSO introduced modified gross national income (GNI*) in 2017 to strip out their effects.

notes.b: Farming is Ireland's main primary activity, and its pattern follows the climate. Mild, wet weather suits grass, so animals matter more than crops.
points: The Census of Agriculture 2020 counted about 135,000 farms, averaging about 33 hectares.
Grass grows for most of the year because winters are mild and rain is reliable, so grass-based livestock farming dominates.
Pastoral farming is livestock farming: beef and dairy cattle, sheep and pigs. The national cattle herd is about 7 million (2020s), which is why beef and dairy cattle are central to farming.
Arable (tillage) farming grows crops: barley is the largest tillage crop, with wheat, oats and potatoes also grown.
Tillage is concentrated in the south and east, in Counties Wexford, Carlow, Kildare, Meath and Cork.
notes.tip: Pastoral means livestock, not crops; arable or tillage means crops. Exams use true or false on this, and ask you to name two crops.

notes.h: Dairy and beef: exports and environmental costs
notes.b: Livestock farming earns money abroad, but a large herd also damages the environment. Exams ask for a benefit and a problem.
points: EU milk quotas (limits on how much milk each country could produce) ended on 1 April 2015, and dairy cow numbers and milk output rose strongly afterwards.
About 90% of Irish beef and dairy output is exported (Bord Bia, 2020s).
A large cattle herd brings exports, food-processing jobs and incomes to rural areas.
Agriculture is the largest single source of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions (gases that warm the atmosphere), about 38% (EPA, 2022 data), with methane from livestock a main part of this.
Nitrate and phosphate runoff (fertiliser and slurry washed from fields) pollutes rivers and lakes, and livestock release ammonia.
notes.tip: For the benefit of a large cattle herd, give exports, food-processing jobs or rural incomes. For an environmental problem, name methane and greenhouse gases or nitrate and phosphate runoff into rivers and lakes.

notes.b: Agri-food means food and drink made from farm produce. Irish brands turn farm output into exports, and exams ask for one food and one drink product.
points: Kerrygold butter is exported by Ornua, the dairy co-operatives' export company; the brand was launched in 1962.
Kerry Group (headquarters Tralee, Co. Kerry) and Glanbia (headquarters Kilkenny) are major food companies, such as those that process Irish farm output.
Tayto crisps were first made in 1954 by Joe 'Spud' Murphy.
Bord Bia, the Irish food board, promotes Irish food, so its exports are better known abroad.
Guinness is made at St James's Gate Brewery, Dublin, a site dating from 1759.
Jameson Irish whiskey is made at Midleton Distillery, Co. Cork; its producer, Irish Distillers, is owned by Pernod Ricard.
Baileys Irish Cream was launched in 1974.
notes.tip: You are asked for one food product and one beverage. Give a named product, such as Kerrygold butter and Guinness.

notes.b: Ireland's geography gives it good conditions for fishing. Several harbours are officially designated as fishing centres.
points: Ireland has a long, indented coastline with sheltered harbours, so boats can land fish safely, and a wide continental shelf (shallow seabed around the coast where fish feed).
Plankton-rich waters and the North Atlantic Drift (a warm ocean current) support productive stocks, especially pelagic (surface-swimming) fish such as mackerel.
Six State Fishery Harbour Centres: Killybegs (Co. Donegal), Castletownbere (Co. Cork), Dingle (Co. Kerry), Rossaveel (Co. Galway), Dunmore East (Co. Waterford) and Howth (Co. Dublin).
Killybegs is Ireland's largest fishing port and lands mainly pelagic fish, such as mackerel.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the Irish sea fisheries board, so it is the State body for the industry.
notes.tip: Exams ask for two fishing ports, so learn two of the six harbour centres, and for the advantages Ireland has for fishing.

notes.h: Fishing: quotas and value to the economy
notes.b: Irish fishing is limited by EU rules, but it still matters to the coastal places that depend on it.
points: The EU Common Fisheries Policy (1983) sets fishing quotas (limits on the catch) for member states, so Irish boats cannot catch as much as they wish.
The 2020 EU–UK Brexit trade agreement reduced Irish quotas, which means Irish fishers may catch less.
Mackerel is the most valuable species landed in Ireland, which is why pelagic waters matter so much.
Fishing earns export income, provides jobs in remote coastal communities and supports fish processing.
notes.tip: For one advantage of fishing to the economy, give exports, jobs in remote coastal communities or fish processing. Do not give a quota percentage or export value.

notes.b: Ireland has little forest, which limits how much wood can be processed. This also explains why the wood industry employs few people.
points: Forest cover is about 11% (2020s), among the lowest in the EU, so there is little timber to process.
Coillte, the State forestry company, was set up in 1988; Sitka spruce is the main plantation tree.

Wood processing employs few people because the forest area is small, plantations are young, sawmills and board mills (which make boards from wood) are highly mechanised (done by machines), and timber is partly exported unprocessed.
Coillte's board mills are Medite, making MDF (medium-density fibreboard) at Clonmel, Co. Tipperary, and SmartPly, making oriented strand board at Belview, Co. Kilkenny, on Waterford Port.
notes.tip: To explain why wood processing employs few people, give the reasons: small forest area, young plantations, highly mechanised mills, and timber partly exported unprocessed.

notes.b: Ireland also takes metal and energy from the ground. The examples below are the named ones to know, one for each.
points: Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, is Europe's largest zinc mine; it opened in 1977 and is owned by Boliden. Production was paused from July 2023 and restarted at the end of 2024.
The Corrib gas field off Co. Mayo first flowed in December 2015, so it is Ireland's example of gas extraction.
ESB's peat-fired power stations at Shannonbridge (West Offaly) and Lanesborough (Lough Ree) closed in December 2020.
Bord na Móna's peat harvesting for electricity has ended, because the peat stations it supplied have closed.

notes.b: Manufacturing in Ireland is driven by foreign companies. The reasons they come are also the answer to 'factors that attract industry to Ireland'.
points: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by foreign companies that set up or expand plants and offices in Ireland.
IDA client companies, mostly foreign-owned, employ about 300,000 people (2023), which shows how much jobs depend on FDI.
Low corporation tax, IDA grants and serviced sites (land already supplied with roads, power and water) attract firms to Ireland.
A young, educated, English-speaking workforce gives firms access to skilled labour.
Access to the EU single market and clusters of similar firms add to the attraction, since suppliers and skills are nearby.
Ireland's time zone, between the USA and Asia, suits firms that serve both.
notes.tip: If asked for one factor attracting industry to Ireland, choose one of these and give its reason. Short questions also ask for two challenges, which are in the block on challenges facing Irish industry.

notes.b: Pharmaceuticals (medicines) and chemicals are the biggest manufacturing sector in Ireland. Cork Harbour is the main centre.
points: Cork Harbour, especially Ringaskiddy and Little Island, is one of the world's largest concentrations of pharmaceutical and chemical plants.
Pfizer, Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) and Novartis have plants at Ringaskiddy; Eli Lilly is at Kinsale, Co. Cork; Pfizer also has a site at Grange Castle, Clondalkin, Dublin.
Pharmaceuticals and chemicals are Ireland's largest goods exports, about half or more of the total (2020s).
notes.tip: Exams ask about the dominance of pharmaceuticals and electronics in Irish industry, so learn the Cork Harbour plants and their share of goods exports.

notes.b: Medical technology and electronics are the other main manufacturing sectors, each centred on named places.
points: Galway is one of Europe's leading medical-technology clusters: Boston Scientific opened there in 1994 and Medtronic is at Parkmore.
Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare, opened in 1989 and is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Fab 34 at Leixlip opened in 2023 and makes advanced chips using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography (printing very fine circuits with a short-wavelength light).
Apple's European headquarters at Hollyhill, Cork, opened in 1980 and employs about 6,000 staff (2020s), so it is a major employer in the city.
notes.tip: Keep the dates straight: Intel opened in Leixlip in 1989, and Apple in Cork in 1980.

notes.b: Not all Irish industry is foreign-owned. Indigenous (Irish-owned) firms get State support, and some have become multinationals themselves.
points: Enterprise Ireland, set up in 1998, supports Irish-owned firms, so they can grow as well as the foreign ones.
Irish-founded firms that grew into multinationals include CRH (building materials) and Smurfit Kappa (paper packaging), which merged with WestRock in 2024 as Smurfit Westrock.
Ryanair, an Irish-founded airline, is a tertiary firm because it provides a transport service.
Ireland has a dual economy: a highly productive foreign-owned sector sits beside a smaller, lower-productivity Irish-owned sector.

notes.b: Ireland's industrial success rests on a few foreign firms and favourable conditions. Each challenge below puts one of those at risk.
points: Dependence on a few large US multinationals means that a single firm's decisions can change output and jobs.
The 15% global minimum tax for very large groups reduces the advantage of Ireland's low rate. There is more on this in the block on the Single Market, euro and corporation tax.
In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice ruled that Apple must pay Ireland about €13 billion plus interest in back taxes; the case had been begun by the European Commission in 2016.
US trade and tax policy changes: the USA raised tariffs on EU goods in 2025.
Brexit: the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and the transition ended on 31 December 2020, changing trade, supply chains and access to the UK market.
High housing and living costs make it hard to attract staff, because workers cannot afford to live near the jobs.
Electricity grid and water constraints, and high energy costs, limit expansion.
Competition from lower-cost countries, because they can make goods more cheaply.
notes.tip: Exams ask for two challenges facing Irish industry. Pick two and give each with its effect. Do not quote the Brexit quota cut or a US tariff rate.

notes.b: A footloose industry is not tied to a location by raw materials or power, so it can locate almost anywhere. This freedom is why governments compete to attract it.
points: Footloose firms choose places with skilled labour, good communications, quality of life and government incentives, because none of these is fixed by nature.
Services such as software, internet and data processing are the most footloose, since their product is information that needs no bulky raw materials.

notes.b: The Dublin region is Ireland's main example of an area dominated by services and footloose industry. Its best-known cluster is Silicon Docks.
points: Silicon Docks is the Grand Canal Dock area, south of the River Liffey, where digital firms cluster.
Microsoft has been in Ireland since 1985; Google has had its European headquarters in Dublin since 2003, at Barrow Street on Grand Canal Dock.
Meta (Facebook), LinkedIn and Salesforce also have large Dublin offices.
The Dublin Docklands Development Authority, set up in 1997, was created to plan and regenerate the docklands.
notes.tip: Silicon Docks is on the south side of the Liffey at Grand Canal Dock. The IFSC is on the north bank, so do not mix them.

notes.h: Why the Dublin region clusters service firms
notes.b: Service firms are footloose, so they go where conditions suit them. Dublin offers several at once.
points: Skilled graduates come from Trinity College Dublin, UCD, DCU, TU Dublin and Maynooth University.
Firms recruit staff from across the EU for offices serving Europe, so language and skills are not limited to Ireland.
Dublin Airport, with over 30 million passengers a year (2023), and fibre connectivity (high-speed internet cables) link the region to the world.
A low tax rate and government incentives attract firms, because they cut costs.
Agglomeration: firms gain from being close to each other, sharing skills and suppliers, so one firm attracts others.
notes.tip: In a 30-mark answer on service and footloose industries, give reasons, effects and problems, with dated examples such as Silicon Docks.

notes.h: Effects of the Dublin service cluster
notes.b: Clustering brings both gains and strains to the Dublin region.
points: The cluster provides high-paid jobs in offices and related services.
Demand for offices and housing has pushed rents up, because supply cannot keep pace.
The concentration of firms and workers adds to congestion (crowded roads and transport) in Dublin.

notes.b: Data centres are buildings full of computers that store and process internet data. They are a newer footloose service, and they put heavy demand on the electricity supply.
points: Data centres used about a fifth (about 21%) of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), and most are in the Dublin region.
A cool climate reduces cooling costs, so running the machines is cheaper; fibre links connect them to global networks; firms cluster near each other; and tax is favourable.
The problem is electricity demand: EirGrid (the national electricity grid operator) stated in 2022 that it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin region until about 2028.

notes.h: Shannon Free Zone and aircraft leasing
notes.b: Shannon was an early planned zone for footloose industry. Its duty-free shop (1947) came before the Free Zone (1959).
points: Brendan O'Regan opened the world's first duty-free airport shop at Shannon in 1947.
The Shannon Free Airport Development Company (SFADCo) was set up in 1959, and the Shannon Free Zone that year offered firms tax relief and duty-free import of components, which cut their costs.
Aircraft leasing (renting planes to airlines) grew from Shannon after Guinness Peat Aviation (GPA) was founded there in 1975 by Tony Ryan, who co-founded Ryanair in the 1980s.
Ireland now manages about half of the world's leased commercial aircraft (2020s, approximately).
notes.tip: Do not merge the dates: the duty-free shop is 1947 and the Free Zone is 1959.

notes.b: Silicon Valley is the original region of footloose high-technology and service industry. It is the global comparison for Dublin.
points: It covers the Santa Clara Valley and the southern San Francisco Bay Area; the name comes from the silicon used in microchips.
Stanford University at Palo Alto encouraged spin-off firms (new firms started by its staff and graduates) and set up Stanford Research Park in 1951.
Hewlett-Packard was founded in a Palo Alto garage in 1939; Intel was founded in Mountain View in 1968 and is now headquartered in Santa Clara.
Apple is based in Cupertino and Google in Mountain View, which shows how the valley hosts the biggest firms.
Problems: very high house prices and rents, traffic congestion, and homelessness alongside great wealth.

notes.b: Financial services are a highly footloose, high-value tertiary activity. They deal in money rather than goods.
points: They include banking, insurance, fund administration, asset management (looking after investments for clients), aircraft leasing, payments and fintech (technology used to deliver financial services).

notes.b: The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) is Ireland's main financial services case study. It was set up to bring in finance and to revive a run-down area.
points: The IFSC was set up in 1987 by the Charles Haughey government on the derelict Custom House Docks, on the north bank of the Liffey.
Approved firms paid a 10% corporation tax rate, so the IFSC was cheaper than elsewhere, later replaced by the 12.5% national rate.
Firms were attracted by the low tax rate, government incentives, an educated English-speaking workforce, EU access, the time zone, and the chance to regenerate a declining dock area.
notes.tip: The IFSC tax rate was 10%, not 12.5%. Use IFSC 1987 as a dated example in a 30-mark answer on financial services.

notes.b: The IFSC grew into a major international centre and changed the area around it.
points: The IFSC became one of the world's largest centres for investment funds (pooled savings invested for clients); Irish-domiciled funds held over €3 trillion in assets (2020s, Central Bank of Ireland).
Aircraft leasing is a second specialism. There is more on this in the block on the Shannon Free Zone and aircraft leasing.
Effects: high-value jobs and the regeneration of the north docklands, served by the Luas Red Line from 2004, with new housing nearby.

notes.b: Finance brings risks as well as gains, but Brexit also created an opening for Dublin.
points: The 2008 banking crisis damaged confidence in Irish finance, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.
After the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin, an opportunity for Ireland.

notes.b: London is the older and larger financial centre against which Dublin can be compared.
points: The City of London (the Square Mile) was deregulated (its rules relaxed) by the 'Big Bang' of the London Stock Exchange in October 1986.
Canary Wharf, built on derelict London docks from the late 1980s, became a second financial district.
After Brexit, some banks moved EU operations from London to Dublin, Frankfurt and Paris.

notes.b: Tourism is a tertiary activity, and whether an area develops it depends on a mix of natural and human factors.
points: Physical attractions: climate, coast, scenery, mountains and lakes.
Cultural and historic attractions: heritage sites, language, music, festivals and sport.
Access: airports, ports, roads and low-cost airlines.
Accommodation and services, and marketing by government agencies.
Cost and exchange rates, and safety and political stability.

notes.b: Tourism brings overseas visitors and supports jobs. State agencies develop it and market it abroad.
points: About 11 million overseas visits were made to the Republic of Ireland in 2019 (CSO).
Tourism supported about a quarter of a million jobs in 2019 (industry estimate), which means it is a major employer.
Britain, the USA and continental Europe (Germany, France) are the main source markets, so most visitors come from these.
Fáilte Ireland, set up in 2003, develops tourism in the Republic; Tourism Ireland, an all-island marketing body created under the Good Friday Agreement (1998), markets the island abroad.
The Wild Atlantic Way, launched in 2014, runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen to Kinsale; Ireland's Ancient East was launched in 2015.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one advantage of tourism. Give jobs, with its link to remote areas, and use the year with any figure.

notes.b: Tourism depends on people being free to travel, so it is exposed to sudden shocks.
points: Overseas visits collapsed in 2020–2021 during COVID-19 travel restrictions, because people could not travel.
Job losses, closed hotels and lost revenue hit remote areas that depend on visitors.
notes.tip: Questions ask why visitor numbers fell in 2020–2021 and one challenge caused by fewer tourists. Give the travel restrictions as the cause, then job losses, closed hotels and lost revenue.

notes.b: Visitors arrive by air or sea, so access is a main factor in tourism. Exams ask you to name an airport and a ferry port.
points: International airports: Dublin, Shannon, Cork, Ireland West Airport Knock (opened 1986) and Kerry Airport at Farranfore.
Ferry ports: Dublin Port (to Holyhead), Rosslare Europort (to Fishguard and Pembroke, and since Brexit more direct routes to France) and Port of Cork at Ringaskiddy (to Roscoff, France).
Ryanair, Europe's largest airline by passengers (2020s), is headquartered in Swords, Co. Dublin.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name an Irish airport and a ferry port, so learn one of each with its route.

notes.h: Why the east coast attracts most visitors
notes.b: More overseas visitors arrive on the east coast than anywhere else. The reasons all come back to Dublin.
points: Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are the main entry points for overseas visitors.
Dublin is the capital, with the most attractions, hotels and events.
Short trips, such as city breaks, suit visitors who arrive in Dublin.
Good motorway and rail links radiate from Dublin, so visitors can reach other places easily.
notes.tip: This is a set question: why the east coast attracts more visitors. Give the entry points first, then the attractions, city breaks and transport links.

notes.b: These are named east-coast attractions you can use when asked for two Irish tourist attractions.
points: The Guinness Storehouse, opened in 2000, is Ireland's most visited fee-paying attraction.
The Book of Kells is at Trinity College Dublin; Dublin Zoo is in the Phoenix Park.
Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), Co. Meath, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place listed by the United Nations as of world importance) since 1993.
The Glendalough monastic site and Powerscourt are both in Co. Wicklow.
notes.tip: When asked to name two attractions, give the place and its county, and do not quote visitor numbers.

notes.h: Attractions on the west and north coasts
notes.b: The west and north coasts have scenic attractions for visitors.
points: The Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are part of the Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark.
Kylemore Abbey is in Connemara, for example as a west-coast attraction.
The Giant's Causeway, Co. Antrim, in Northern Ireland, has been a UNESCO site since 1986.

notes.b: Co. Kerry, centred on Killarney and the Ring of Kerry, is a mass-tourism region, meaning large numbers of visitors come there. Its scenery, heritage and access combine to draw them.
points: Killarney National Park, created in 1932 from the Muckross estate, was Ireland's first national park; the estate was given to the State by the Bourn Vincent family.
Attractions include Muckross House, the Lakes of Killarney, Torc Waterfall, the Gap of Dunloe and Ross Castle.
Carrauntoohil (1,038 m), in the Macgillycuddy's Reeks, is Ireland's highest mountain.
The Ring of Kerry is a circular route of about 180 km around the Iveragh Peninsula.

Skellig Michael, an early Christian monastery on a rocky island, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996 and was a film location for Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) and The Last Jedi (2017).
The Dingle Peninsula, with the Slea Head drive and the Dingle Gaeltacht (an Irish-speaking area), adds to the county's attractions.
notes.tip: Killarney National Park is not a UNESCO site; Skellig Michael is. Kerry Airport at Farranfore provides air access.

notes.b: Kerry has attracted visitors for a long time, and better transport helped.
points: Tourism in Killarney dates from the 18th and 19th centuries.
The railway reached Killarney in 1853, bringing more visitors by making travel easier.
Queen Victoria visited Killarney in 1861, which helped publicise it.

notes.b: Tourism changes a region in good and bad ways. Exams ask for positive and negative impacts in a named region.
points: Positive: jobs and income in a peripheral region (one far from the main centres), services kept open in rural areas, and heritage protected through tourism income.
Negative: seasonal jobs, with work concentrated in the summer months.
Negative: traffic and coach congestion on the narrow roads of the Ring of Kerry.
Negative: erosion on the Carrauntoohil paths and litter on popular trails.
Negative: holiday homes push up house prices and make affordable housing scarce for local workers.
notes.tip: For positive and negative impacts in a region, use Kerry examples, such as jobs, congestion on the Ring of Kerry and holiday homes.

notes.b: Spain is the European example of mass tourism on a large scale. Its growth had specific causes.
points: Spain received about 84 million international tourists in 2019 and about 94 million in 2024, a record (INE, the Spanish statistics office).
Tourism provides over a tenth of Spain's GDP (2020s, approximate).
Mass tourism grew from the 1960s under the Franco regime, which promoted it with the 'Spain is different' slogan to earn foreign currency.
Causes: sun and beaches; package holidays and jet aircraft; cheap flights; low costs; and proximity to northern Europe.

notes.b: Spain's Mediterranean coasts and islands hold the main resorts.
points: Benidorm, on the Costa Blanca, was a small fishing village transformed in the 1950s and 1960s by mayor Pedro Zaragoza's plan for high-rise buildings close to the beach.
The Gran Hotel Bali (186 m, opened 2002) was then Europe's tallest hotel.
The Costa del Sol has Málaga airport, so visitors arrive by air at Torremolinos and Marbella.
The Balearic Islands, in the Mediterranean, include Mallorca (Palma, Magaluf) and Ibiza.
notes.tip: The Balearic Islands are in the Mediterranean; the Canary Islands are in the Atlantic off Africa. Do not place Benidorm, Torremolinos or Magaluf in the Canaries.

notes.b: Mass tourism brought money to Spain, but it also caused problems, now met with protest.
points: Effects: jobs, foreign earnings and infrastructure, such as airports and roads.
Problems: 'ribbon development' (a strip of concrete buildings along the coast), and high-rise overdevelopment.
Water shortages: Catalonia declared a drought emergency in early 2024.
Low-paid seasonal jobs, and rising rents as short-term tourist lets spread.
Large anti-overtourism protests took place in 2024 in Barcelona, Mallorca and the Canary Islands.

notes.b: Governments in Spain have started to limit the effects of tourism.
points: The Balearic and Catalan governments charge tourist taxes.
Barcelona plans to end licences for about 10,000 tourist apartments by 2028.

notes.b: Industries do not last forever. Industrial decline is a downward trend, and it leaves visible signs.
points: Industrial decline is the long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region.
Evidence: plant closures, derelict sites and buildings, high unemployment, emigration (out-migration), falling population in industrial towns, and social problems.
notes.tip: Evidence and causes of industrial decline is a Higher Level 30-mark topic, sometimes combined with a named region. Give the definition and evidence first.

notes.b: Irish industry declined for several reasons. Each reason is illustrated by the dated examples that follow.
points: The end of protection and the opening to free trade exposed small, inefficient protected firms, through the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) and EEC membership (1973).
Competition from low-wage countries, because they can sell more cheaply.
Recessions (periods when the economy shrinks), such as those of the 1980s and 2008.
New technology replacing labour, so fewer workers are needed.
EU policy reform, such as the reform of the EU sugar regime.
Corporate decisions to move production to lower-cost locations, as with Dell in Limerick. There is more on this in the Irish examples blocks.

notes.b: Cork lost several large employers in the 1980s, during a recession.
points: The Dunlop tyre factory in Cork closed in 1983.
Ford's Marina plant in Cork closed in 1984; Ford's Cork company was founded in 1917.
Verolme Cork Dockyard at Rushbrooke closed in 1984.

notes.h: Steel, sugar, crystal and computer closures, 2001 to 2009
notes.b: Further closures followed in the 2000s, each with a different cause. Dates matter here.
points: Irish Steel (later Ispat) closed on Haulbowline Island, Cork Harbour, in 2001; the site needed a costly clean-up of contaminated waste.
Irish Sugar (Greencore) closed its Carlow beet factory in 2005 and its Mallow factory in 2006, ending Irish sugar production after EU sugar-regime reform.
Waterford Crystal's Kilbarry factory closed in January 2009 when the company went into receivership (when an outside manager takes control of a company that cannot pay its debts).
Dell opened at Raheen, Limerick, in 1990; in January 2009 it announced that manufacturing would move to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs, while sales and service stayed in Ireland.
notes.tip: Dell opened in Limerick in 1990, and its 2009 move to Poland is here a single example of decline. Do not swap it with Intel in 1989 or Apple in 1980.

notes.h: Moneypoint and the end of coal
notes.b: Energy industries also declined as Ireland moved away from fossil fuels (fuels such as coal and peat, formed from ancient plants).
points: Moneypoint, Co. Clare, a coal-fired power station built in the 1980s, was Ireland's last coal-burning power station.
Coal burning at Moneypoint ended in 2025, so Ireland no longer burns coal for power, part of the move away from fossil fuels that also closed the peat stations.

notes.b: When industries close, the damage spreads from the workers to the whole town.
points: Unemployment reached about 17% in the mid-1980s.
Heavy emigration in the 1980s drew skilled people away from the affected towns, because there were no jobs for them.
Derelict docklands and empty factories were left in city and town centres.
Local towns lost skills and spending as jobs disappeared.

notes.b: Governments and agencies tried to replace lost jobs and reuse empty sites.
points: Replacement investment: the IDA and Enterprise Ireland sought new firms to replace lost jobs.
Regeneration (rebuilding and renewing run-down areas) of the Dublin Docklands and the IFSC. There is more on this in the IFSC blocks.
Regeneration of Cork Docklands, through a city plan to redevelop the old port quays.
Heritage reuse: a smaller House of Waterford Crystal factory and visitor centre opened in Waterford city centre (the Mall) in 2010.
Retraining for displaced workers, so they can move into new jobs.
The EU Just Transition Fund supports the Midlands peat region, because peat jobs have ended.

notes.b: Ireland is not alone in losing traditional industry.
points: There is more on coalfield and steel regions of decline elsewhere in Europe in the Socio-economic regions notes.

notes.b: Economic activity is unevenly spread across Ireland. Some regions have far more jobs and income than others.
points: The Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State's population, and holds most multinational and service jobs, along with Cork, Galway and Limerick.
The Border, Midlands and West have more small farms, fewer FDI jobs and lower incomes.
The Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region was designated for EU funding in 1999 (Objective 1 for 2000–2006); the rest of the State was the Southern and Eastern region.
The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040, 2018) aims for Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford to each grow by at least 50% by 2040, to balance growth away from Dublin.

keyTerms.definition: Economic activity that extracts raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
Economic activity that processes raw materials or assembles components into goods, including construction.
Economic activity that provides services, such as banking, tourism, teaching and transport.
Farming that rears livestock, such as beef and dairy cattle, sheep and pigs.
Arable farming that grows crops, such as barley, wheat, oats and potatoes.
Investment by a foreign company that sets up or expands plants or offices in Ireland.
An economy with a highly productive foreign-owned sector beside a smaller, less productive Irish-owned sector.
An industry not tied to one location by raw materials or power, so it can locate almost anywhere.
The advantage firms gain by clustering near each other, sharing skills and suppliers.
The International Financial Services Centre, set up in Dublin in 1987 on the derelict Custom House Docks.
The long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region.
Building in a continuous strip along a coastline or road, typical of coastal resorts.
Protest against so many visitors that local residents, housing and services are placed under pressure.

factCards.term: Ireland from protection to free trade, 1932 to 1973
factCards.definition: Protection: the Control of Manufactures Acts (1932, 1934) and high tariffs shielded Irish firms, leaving 1950s unemployment and emigration. Opening: IDA 1949; Export Profits Tax Relief 1956; Whitaker's First Programme 1958; Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement 1965; EEC 1973.

factCards.term: How Ireland built a skilled, open economy after 1966: four dated steps
factCards.definition: Free second-level education (announced 1966 by Donogh O'Malley, introduced 1967) built an educated workforce; the EU Single Market began in 1993; the euro came in 1999 (notes and coins 2002); corporation tax on trading profits was 12.5% from 2003.

factCards.term: Celtic Tiger, mid-1990s to 2007: causes and effects
factCards.definition: Driven first by exports and FDI, especially US technology and pharmaceutical firms, then by a property and construction boom. Unemployment fell to about 4–5% by the mid-2000s; net immigration replaced emigration, with large inflows from new EU states after 2004.

factCards.term: Irish banking crash: the sequence of events, 2007 to 2013
factCards.definition: Property bubble burst 2007–2008; bank guarantee 30 September 2008; Anglo Irish Bank nationalised January 2009; NAMA set up later in 2009 to take over property loans; EU–IMF programme of €67.5 billion in external loans agreed November 2010, exited December 2013.

factCards.term: Why the Irish government built up such a large debt after 2008
factCards.definition: The state borrowed heavily to rescue the banks (bank guarantee 2008, Anglo Irish Bank nationalised 2009, EU–IMF loans 2010) while its tax base collapsed with the property crash, so government debt peaked at about 120% of GDP in 2012.

factCards.term: Five benefits of high employment to an economy
factCards.definition: More income-tax and VAT revenue; lower welfare spending; consumer spending that supports jobs in other sectors; less emigration, so skilled people stay; more government money to invest in infrastructure and services.

factCards.term: Irish agriculture: key figures and where tillage is concentrated
factCards.definition: Census of Agriculture 2020: about 135,000 farms averaging about 33 hectares; about 7 million cattle (2020s). Mild winters and reliable rain favour grass-based livestock. Barley is the largest tillage crop; tillage is concentrated in Wexford, Carlow, Kildare, Meath and Cork.

factCards.term: Ireland's large cattle herd: benefits and environmental problems
factCards.definition: Benefits: exports (about 90% of beef and dairy output), food-processing jobs, rural incomes; dairying grew after milk quotas ended on 1 April 2015. Problems: methane makes agriculture Ireland's largest source of greenhouse gases, about 38% (EPA, 2022 data); nitrate and phosphate runoff; ammonia.

factCards.term: Name an Irish food product and an Irish drink, with their makers
factCards.definition: Food: Kerrygold butter (Ornua, launched 1962); Tayto crisps (first made 1954 by Joe 'Spud' Murphy). Drink: Guinness (brewed at St James's Gate, Dublin, since 1759); Jameson whiskey (Irish Distillers, Midleton, Co. Cork); Baileys Irish Cream (launched 1974).

factCards.term: Irish fishing: natural advantages and value to the economy
factCards.definition: Advantages: a long, indented coastline with sheltered harbours; a wide continental shelf; plankton-rich waters and the North Atlantic Drift; pelagic stocks, mackerel being the most valuable. Value: exports, jobs in remote coastal communities, fish processing.

factCards.term: Name Ireland's six State Fishery Harbour Centres
factCards.definition: Killybegs (Co. Donegal), the largest, landing mainly pelagic fish; Castletownbere (Co. Cork); Dingle (Co. Kerry); Rossaveel (Co. Galway); Dunmore East (Co. Waterford); Howth (Co. Dublin).

factCards.term: Ireland's main manufacturing sectors: a location and firm for each
factCards.definition: Pharmaceuticals and chemicals, the largest goods exports: Cork Harbour (Pfizer, Janssen, Novartis at Ringaskiddy). Medical devices: Galway (Boston Scientific 1994, Medtronic). ICT: Intel, Leixlip (1989); Apple, Cork (1980). Food and drink: Kerry Group (Tralee) and Glanbia (Kilkenny).

factCards.term: Challenges facing industry in Ireland: name seven
factCards.definition: Dependence on a few US multinationals; the 15% minimum tax for very large groups (2024); US tariffs on EU goods (2025); Brexit; housing costs that deter staff; grid and water limits (EirGrid will not connect new Dublin data centres until about 2028); lower-cost rivals.

factCards.term: Silicon Docks, Dublin: where it is, named firms and effects
factCards.definition: Grand Canal Dock, south of the Liffey. Google has had its European headquarters in Dublin since 2003, now on Barrow Street; Meta and LinkedIn also have large offices in the area. Effects: high-paid jobs, rising rents, congestion.

factCards.term: Why service and footloose firms cluster in the Dublin region
factCards.definition: Graduates from Trinity College Dublin, UCD, DCU, TU Dublin and Maynooth University; EU-wide recruitment; Dublin Airport (over 30 million passengers, 2023) and fibre links; low tax and incentives; agglomeration, as firms share skills and suppliers.

factCards.term: Shannon: duty-free shop, Free Zone and aircraft leasing
factCards.definition: Brendan O'Regan opened the world's first duty-free airport shop at Shannon in 1947; the Shannon Free Zone (1959) gave firms tax relief and duty-free imports. Tony Ryan founded GPA at Shannon in 1975; Ireland now manages about half the world's leased aircraft.

factCards.term: Silicon Valley, California: origins, named firms and problems
factCards.definition: Stanford University encouraged spin-off firms and opened its Research Park in 1951; Hewlett-Packard began in a Palo Alto garage in 1939; Intel (founded 1968) is headquartered in Santa Clara; Apple is at Cupertino, Google at Mountain View. Problems: high house prices, congestion, homelessness.

factCards.term: IFSC, Dublin: when, where and why it was set up
factCards.definition: Set up in 1987 by the Charles Haughey government on the derelict Custom House Docks, north of the Liffey. Reasons: a 10% tax rate for approved firms, government incentives, an educated English-speaking workforce, EU access, the time zone, and regeneration of the docks.

factCards.term: IFSC: growth, effects and the Brexit opportunity
factCards.definition: Irish-domiciled funds hold over €3 trillion (2020s). Effects: high-value jobs; regeneration of the north docklands, served by the Luas Red Line (2004). After the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin.

factCards.term: Factors that influence the development of tourism in an area
factCards.definition: Physical attractions (climate, coast, scenery); cultural and historic attractions (heritage, music, festivals, sport); access (airports, ports, low-cost airlines); accommodation and services; marketing; cost and exchange rates; safety and political stability.

factCards.term: Irish tourism: its importance and the COVID-19 collapse
factCards.definition: About 11 million overseas visits and about a quarter of a million jobs (2019); main markets Britain, the USA, Germany and France. COVID-19 travel restrictions collapsed visits in 2020–2021, causing job losses, closed hotels and lost revenue in remote areas.

factCards.term: Irish tourism agencies and marketing brands
factCards.definition: Fáilte Ireland (2003) develops tourism in the Republic; Tourism Ireland, created under the Good Friday Agreement (1998), markets the whole island. The Wild Atlantic Way (2014) runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen to Kinsale; Ireland's Ancient East followed in 2015.

factCards.term: Why Ireland's east coast attracts the most visitors
factCards.definition: Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are the main entry points; Dublin, the capital, has the most attractions, hotels and events; city breaks suit short trips; good motorway and rail links radiate from Dublin.

factCards.term: Irish tourist attractions: four in the east and two in the west
factCards.definition: East: the Guinness Storehouse (2000), the most visited fee-paying attraction; the Book of Kells, Trinity College Dublin; Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), UNESCO 1993; Glendalough, Co. Wicklow. West: the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare; Kylemore Abbey, Connemara.

factCards.term: Co. Kerry as a mass-tourism region: main attractions
factCards.definition: Killarney National Park (1932), Ireland's first, from the Muckross estate; the Lakes of Killarney, Torc Waterfall, Gap of Dunloe; Carrauntoohil (1,038 m), Ireland's highest mountain; the Ring of Kerry (about 180 km); Skellig Michael (UNESCO 1996).

factCards.term: Co. Kerry tourism: positive and negative impacts
factCards.definition: Positive: jobs and income in a peripheral region; rural services kept open; heritage protected. Negative: seasonal jobs; coach congestion on the narrow Ring of Kerry roads; erosion on Carrauntoohil paths and litter; holiday homes raising house prices for locals.

factCards.term: Spain's mass tourism: causes of its growth
factCards.definition: From the 1960s the Franco regime promoted tourism ('Spain is different') to earn foreign currency; jet aircraft and package holidays, later cheap flights; sun and beaches; low costs; nearness to northern Europe. About 84 million tourists in 2019; about 94 million in 2024.

factCards.term: Benidorm and other mass-tourism resorts in Spain
factCards.definition: Benidorm, Costa Blanca: a fishing village transformed in the 1950s–60s by mayor Pedro Zaragoza's high-rise plan; the Gran Hotel Bali (186 m, 2002) was then Europe's tallest hotel. Costa del Sol: Torremolinos, Marbella. Balearics: Mallorca (Magaluf), Ibiza.

factCards.term: Spain's mass tourism: four problems
factCards.definition: Concrete ribbon development and high-rise overbuilding on coasts; water shortages (Catalonia's drought emergency, early 2024); low-paid seasonal jobs; rents raised by short-term tourist lets, prompting 2024 protests in Barcelona, Mallorca and the Canary Islands.

factCards.term: Spain's mass tourism: economic effects and two responses
factCards.definition: Effects: jobs, foreign earnings and infrastructure; tourism gives over a tenth of Spain's GDP (2020s). Responses: the Balearic and Catalan governments charge tourist taxes; Barcelona plans to end licences for about 10,000 tourist apartments by 2028.

factCards.term: Evidence of industrial decline in a region: give six types
factCards.definition: Plant closures; derelict sites and buildings; high unemployment; emigration or out-migration; falling population in industrial towns; social problems.

factCards.term: Causes of industrial decline in Ireland
factCards.definition: The end of protection exposed small, inefficient firms (Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement 1965, EEC 1973); competition from low-wage countries; recessions (1980s, 2008); new technology replacing labour; EU reform such as the sugar regime; firms moving production abroad.

factCards.term: Cork's 1980s closures and the effects of decline
factCards.definition: Dunlop's tyre factory closed in 1983; Ford's Marina plant and Verolme Cork Dockyard, Rushbrooke, closed in 1984. Effects: job losses in Cork as national unemployment reached about 17% in the mid-1980s; heavy emigration; derelict docklands; lost skills and spending in local towns.

factCards.term: Irish industrial closures since 2001: name five with dates
factCards.definition: Irish Steel, Haulbowline (2001), leaving a contaminated site; Irish Sugar's Carlow (2005) and Mallow (2006) factories after EU sugar reform; Waterford Crystal, Kilbarry (January 2009); Dell manufacturing, Limerick (2009, about 1,900 jobs); peat power stations (2020).

factCards.term: Responses to industrial decline in Ireland
factCards.definition: IDA and Enterprise Ireland replacement investment; regeneration of the Dublin Docklands (Docklands Development Authority 1997, IFSC 1987) and Cork Docklands; heritage reuse, like the House of Waterford Crystal on the Mall (2010); retraining; the EU Just Transition Fund.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the development of financial services in a developed economy you have studied.
questions.model: 1) Origin: the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) was set up in Dublin in 1987. 2) Site: it was built on the derelict Custom House Docks, on the north bank of the Liffey, a declining dock area. 3) Government: the Charles Haughey government created the IFSC and gave it incentives. 4) Tax: approved firms paid a 10% corporation tax rate, later replaced by the 12.5% national rate. 5) Workforce: an educated, English-speaking workforce attracted firms. 6) EU access: a base inside the EU single market suited banks and funds serving Europe. 7) Time zone: Dublin's time zone suited firms working with other financial centres. 8) Growth: the IFSC became one of the world's largest centres for investment funds, with Irish-domiciled funds holding over €3 trillion in assets (2020s). 9) Aircraft leasing: the leasing business grew from Shannon after Guinness Peat Aviation was founded there in 1975, and Ireland now manages about half of the world's leased commercial aircraft (approximately). 10) Effects: high-value jobs and regeneration of the north docklands, with the Luas Red Line (2004) serving the IFSC and new housing nearby. 11) Brexit: after the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin. 12) Risk: the 2008 banking crisis left Anglo Irish Bank nationalised in January 2009 and led to NAMA being set up in 2009 to take over property loans. 13) Reputation: financial services depend on trust, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.

questions.prompt: Examine the evidence of industrial decline in a developed economy you have studied.
questions.model: 1) Definition: industrial decline is the long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region. 2) Evidence: plant closures, derelict sites, high unemployment, emigration and falling population in industrial towns. 3) Cause: the end of protection and the opening to free trade, through the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) and EEC membership (1973), exposed small, inefficient firms. 4) Cause: competition from low-wage countries. 5) Cause: recessions in the 1980s and 2008. 6) Cause: new technology replacing labour. 7) Cause: corporate decisions to move production abroad. 8) Example: the Dunlop tyre factory (1983), Ford's Marina plant (1984) and Verolme Cork Dockyard (1984) closed in Cork. 9) Example: Irish Steel on Haulbowline Island, Cork Harbour, closed in 2001. 10) Example: Irish Sugar closed its Carlow factory in 2005 and its Mallow factory in 2006 after EU sugar-regime reform. 11) Example: Waterford Crystal's Kilbarry factory closed in January 2009. 12) Example: Dell in Limerick announced in 2009 that manufacturing would move to Poland, with about 1,900 jobs lost. 13) Example: the ESB's peat-fired power stations closed in December 2020. 14) Effects: unemployment of about 17% in the mid-1980s, heavy emigration and derelict docklands. 15) Responses: replacement investment by the IDA and Enterprise Ireland, regeneration of the Dublin and Cork docklands, the House of Waterford Crystal visitor centre, retraining, and the EU Just Transition Fund for the Midlands.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one tertiary activity in a developed economy you have studied. (ii) Explain the advantages this economy has for it. (iii) Describe one challenge it faces.
questions.model: (i) Tourism in Ireland. (ii) 1) Physical attractions: scenery, coast, mountains and lakes, such as the Ring of Kerry and Carrauntoohil in Co. Kerry. 2) Heritage: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), a UNESCO site since 1993; Skellig Michael, a UNESCO site since 1996; and the Book of Kells in Dublin. 3) Access: Dublin Airport, Shannon, Cork and Kerry airports, Dublin Port and Rosslare Europort, and low-cost airlines such as Ryanair. 4) Marketing: Tourism Ireland promotes the island abroad, with the Wild Atlantic Way and Ireland's Ancient East as brands. 5) Language: English is widely spoken, which suits visitors from Britain and the USA. 6) Income: tourism brings in overseas earnings and supported about a quarter of a million jobs in 2019. (iii) Challenge: seasonality. 1) Tourism is concentrated in the summer months, so many jobs are seasonal and workers are employed for only part of the year. 2) Busy months bring congestion on roads such as the Ring of Kerry. 3) In quiet months, hotels and attractions are underused, which lowers their income.
